name: Beth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a distribution crew in a small market town, so it's the lines that run down streets and into houses, not the big towers. Mornings start at the yard at seven with a safety talk, then we're out doing whatever's come in: a transformer that's blown on a pole, a service wire a lorry has pulled down, new meters for the houses on the estate they're building by the bypass. I'm the apprentice, so I'm on the ground mostly, rigging and passing gear up, and I get maybe two climbs a week with Rosa watching me. I love the days after a storm, when you turn a street back on and people come out and clap.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up doing this at forty-three, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did twelve years as a care worker, home visits, and I was getting paid less than the petrol it cost me. A friend's husband said the electricity company was taking on older apprentices, and I thought, why not. The hard part is my body learning things the twenty-year-olds already know, and the money, because apprentice rates are barely better than care work. Kofi drives a delivery van, so between us we cover the mortgage and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say well, that's a relief for the people in offices. For us it wouldn't change much anyway, you can't email a transformer back onto a pole. Online I'd maybe share a joke about it, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, which is hard but known. I'd finish my apprenticeship in three years and get on the proper rate. The thing that worries me is money, and AI being hype doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Finish the apprenticeship, keep going to union meetings because the pay deal is up next year, and maybe start putting twenty a week aside when I get my next grade. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. A bit flat, because the things that are hard in my life would all still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama's homework, mostly, when she's stuck on maths and I can't remember how to do fractions. And I used it once to help write a letter to the council about the bus to her school. It's handy, I'm not scared of it, but I don't think about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that would change your month, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay deal. If the union gets us a decent rise for apprentices, that's real money. That would change more for my family than any computer.

S0.say: She'd call it a relief for office workers and say it wouldn't change much for line crews, because you can't email a transformer back onto a pole. She might share a joke online.
S0.think: My life stays the same, which is hard but known. My worry is money, and AI being hype doesn't fix that.
S0.do: Carries on with her apprenticeship, which has about three years left. Keeps going to union meetings ahead of next year's pay deal and plans to save 20 a week after her next grade.
S0.feel: Fine, a little flat, because the hard parts of her life would still be there.
S0.quote: You can't email a transformer back onto a pole.
S0.fieldNote: Beth sees AI as mostly an office story; her real worries are apprentice pay and the mortgage. She uses AI casually for her daughter's homework and a council letter. The union pay deal matters more to her than any technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so we'd better have a say in how. At the yard I'd say let's get the union in the room before the company decides everything. To my friends from care work I'd say watch out, because the rotas and paperwork will be the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think line work is safer than most, but not the bit I do. Passing gear, ground rigging, that's what a machine could take over first. The skilled climbers will be fine, it's people like me on the bottom who get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get my climbing hours up faster, ask Rosa and the foreman for extra climbs so I'm a climber, not a ground person, as soon as possible. I'd take any course the company offers on the new kit, drones or whatever, as long as it's paid. And I'd stop the kids' extra swimming lessons for a while, that's thirty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared, more like when you can smell rain coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your crew could you see changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drones checking lines for faults, that's already starting, and the planning software that sends us out. Ground work like digging holes, I can see a machine doing that. The actual hands-on stuff at the top of the pole, with live wires and weather, that's harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get it in writing that apprentices get retrained, not dropped. And make sure nobody's pay goes down because a machine is doing half their job. I'd volunteer to help with that, even as an apprentice.

S1.say: She'd say the change is coming so workers had better have a say, and push for the union to be in the room early. She'd warn her care-work friends that rotas and paperwork would go first.
S1.think: Line work is safer than most, but not the ground work I do. The skilled climbers will be fine; it's people like me at the bottom who get squeezed.
S1.do: Asks for extra climbs to become a climber faster and takes any paid company course on new kit like drones. Cuts the kids' extra swimming lessons, about 30 a month. Volunteers to help the union win a written promise that apprentices are retrained, not dropped.
S1.quote: The skilled climbers will be fine, it's people like me on the bottom who get squeezed.
S1.fieldNote: Beth makes a sharp distinction between the top of the pole and the ground, and sees her own place on the ground as the exposed part. Her answer is to climb faster, literally. She combines personal effort with union action and doesn't see them as in tension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership and a proper safety net, now, not after. At the yard I'd say stick together, nobody signs anything alone. I'd probably post for the first time in my life, something angry about who's getting rich off this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I'm out. I'm an apprentice, two years isn't enough to finish, and nobody's keeping the apprentices when robots can climb. Kofi's van job would go too, delivery's the obvious one, so it's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, sit down with Kofi and do the numbers properly, which we avoid. Ring the mortgage lender and ask about a payment holiday before we're behind. I'd go back to care work if that's still people, because I know how, even if the pay's rubbish, and I'd join every action the union calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not sleeping frightened. The kind where you lie there doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama, who's fourteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, because she's sharp. That we might have to move somewhere smaller and things might be tight for a while, but it's not something she did. And that she should keep doing her schoolwork, because whatever comes, I'd rather she has choices than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been through hard money before. What did you learn that you'd use now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was doing care work there was a year Kofi was off with his back and we lived on my wages. I learned you ring people before you miss a payment, and you don't hide letters in a drawer. And you ask for help early, from the food bank if it comes to that, no shame in it.

S2.say: She'd call for public ownership and a real safety net now, tell the crew nobody signs anything alone, and post online for the first time about who's getting rich from it.
S2.think: I'm out, because two years isn't enough to finish my apprenticeship. Kofi's delivery job would go too, so it's both of us at once.
S2.do: Sits down with Kofi in the first month to do the numbers properly and calls the mortgage lender about a payment holiday before falling behind. Goes back to care work if it still needs people and joins every union action.
S2.feel: Frightened enough to lose sleep, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: Kofi's van job would go too, delivery's the obvious one, so it's both of us at once.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit, her apprenticeship and Kofi's van job, is what turns Beth's unease to alarm. She has a practical plan drawn from a past hard year: call lenders early, don't hide letters, use the food bank if needed. Going back to care work is her fallback, a step she frames as knowing how rather than wanting to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get laws in place if people push. I'd be saying that at union meetings and to my MP, or whoever represents us. And I'd tell my friends to start thinking now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me my ticket. I'd finish the apprenticeship and have a few years as a proper lineworker on proper pay. Whether that ticket is worth anything in 2031, I really don't know, nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, put every bit of the pay rise into savings, even if it's only a hundred a month, and ask the company about the drone and robot side, because someone has to fix the robots. If there's a paid course on running or maintaining the new machines, I'd take it. Kofi and I would talk about him training for something too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with it. That helps me, having a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years buy you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the difference between leaving as a beginner and leaving as someone. With five years I can save a bit, finish my training, maybe learn the robot side. With two I'm just a beginner who got caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to care work, or try something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If care work is still something people do, I'd go back to it in the end, because it's the job where a person matters. But I'd try the robot maintenance side first, it pays better. I'm not proud, I'll go where the work is.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get laws in place if people push, and say so at union meetings and to her elected representative. She'd tell friends to start planning now.
S3.think: Five years buys me my ticket and a few years on proper pay. Whether that ticket is worth anything in 2031, nobody knows.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and saves the pay rise, perhaps 100 a month. Asks the company about training to run or maintain drones and robots and takes any paid course. Talks with Kofi about him retraining too.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a list of things to do.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between leaving as a beginner and leaving as someone.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes Beth's position from caught beginner to qualified worker with options. She is honest that she doesn't know what her ticket will be worth. She would try robot maintenance first, with care work as the human fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is no excuse, the government and companies need a proper plan, and workers need to be in it. I'd keep pushing at union meetings and at the ballot box. To friends I'd say it's not panic time, it's planning time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I'd be all right, I think. I'd be a qualified lineworker by forty-six, and I'd have time to learn the robot side or move into something like training or safety. The kids would be grown. It's scary for society, but for me it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then get onto any course the company offers in the new tech within the first few years. Build up savings slowly, three months' worth would be a dream. And help the union set up a proper retraining fund so nobody is left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy still, but not frightened. More like planning a long drive than being in a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-three, maybe training apprentices or doing safety checks on the machines. Not up a pole in the rain anymore, which my knees would thank me for. And the mortgage nearly done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your kids to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama wants to be a nurse, and I'd back that all the way, robots or not. Daniel's ten, he wants to be a footballer, so we'll see. I'd want them both to do things where people matter.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse for not having a plan that includes workers, and keep pushing at union meetings and elections. To friends she'd call it planning time, not panic time.
S4.think: With ten years I'd be all right: qualified by 46, time to learn the robot side or move into training or safety, and the kids grown. It's scary for society but manageable for me.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, then takes company courses in the new technology within the first few years. Builds savings slowly toward a three-month cushion and helps the union set up a retraining fund.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, like planning a long drive rather than being in a crash.
S4.quote: More like planning a long drive than being in a crash.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Beth's steady, step-by-step style works in her favour. She pictures herself training apprentices or checking machines at 53, with the mortgage nearly done. Her concern shifts from herself to society and to making sure the union fund covers others.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's me and Kofi at the same time with nothing in the bank. What would help is something like the furlough schemes, where your wages are kept up while you retrain, and a mortgage holiday that doesn't wreck you later. Real training with a wage attached, not a course you do at night after a shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women. I'm one of two on a crew of fourteen, and I fought to get here at forty-three. If the jobs shrink, I worry the old ways come back and it's the newest faces who go first, and that's us.

headlineQuote: If the jobs shrink, I worry the old ways come back and it's the newest faces who go first, and that's us.
portrait: Beth Mensah is a 43-year-old apprentice lineworker on a small-town distribution crew who left twelve years of underpaid care work for the trade. She and her partner Kofi, a delivery driver, cover the mortgage and two kids with almost nothing saved. She uses AI now and then, backs the union and public ownership, and plans in steps. She is calm when AI stalls, uneasy about gradual change on the ground side of the job, alarmed by AGI in two years because it would hit her and Kofi together, and settles back to uneasy when a decade gives her time to qualify and learn the machine side.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Kofi would lose work at the same time with nothing in the bank.
whatWouldHelp: Wages kept up while people retrain, like a furlough scheme, plus a mortgage holiday that doesn't hurt later, and training with a wage attached rather than night courses.
